title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 2
paragraphs: _How King Ryence came to Cameliard, and how King Arthur fought with the Duke of North Umber._

One day around this time, a messenger came to the court of King Leodegrance. He brought news that King Ryence of North Wales and Duke Mordaunt of North Umber were coming, and that they were bringing a large and splendid company of knights and lords. King Leodegrance was deeply troubled by this news. He did not know what the visit meant, but he greatly feared it meant trouble for him. So on the day King Ryence and the Duke of North Umber appeared before the castle, King Leodegrance went out to greet them. The three of them met in the meadows below the castle walls of Cameliard.
There King Leodegrance welcomed the two visitors in the proper manner. He asked them to come into the castle with him, so that he could entertain them as their rank deserved.

But King Ryence gave no friendly answer to this courtesy. “No,” he said, “we will not go with you into your castle, King Leodegrance, until we learn whether you are our friend or our enemy. Right now we are certainly not such good friends with you that we want to sit at your table and eat your bread and salt. And we cannot be anything but your enemies until you have met our demands. You must give me the lands I am asking for, and you must give the Lady Guinevere to my cousin, Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, to be his wife. It is in your power to make us either your friends or your enemies. So we will stay here, outside your castle, for five days. In that time you can decide on your answer, and then we will know whether we are friends or enemies.”

“And in the meantime,” said Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, “I am ready to fight for my right to the hand of the Lady Guinevere against any knight of your court who wants to deny my just claim. And if you have no knight in your whole court who can face me in a bout of arms, you can hardly hope to defend yourself against the great army of knights King Ryence has gathered to bring against you, if you refuse what we ask.”

King Leodegrance was greatly discouraged. He feared those proud lords, and he did not know what to say to them. So he turned and walked back into his castle, weighed down with worry and sorrow. King Ryence and Duke Mordaunt and their court of lords and knights set up their pavilions in the meadows across from the castle, until the whole plain was covered with tents. There they made camp with great rejoicing, with the sounds of feasting and singing and merrymaking, for King Ryence had gathered a very noble court around him.

When the next morning came, Duke Mordaunt of North Umber went out dressed in armor that no weapon could pierce. He rode up and down the field before the castle and loudly challenged those inside, daring any knight to come out and meet him in a knightly fight. “Ho!” he cried. “What now, you Knights of Cameliard! Is there no one to come out and meet me? How can you hope to stand against the Knights of North Wales, if you are afraid to face one single Knight from North Umber?” He mocked them in his pride, and no one dared to come out from Cameliard against him. The Duke of North Umber was one of the most famous knights of his day, and he was very strong and had won many fights. In these peaceful times, no one at King Leodegrance’s court was able to face a warrior of such proven skill and courage. So no one took up the challenge that the Duke of North Umber gave to the court of Cameliard. Meanwhile, many people gathered on the walls of Cameliard and looked down at the proud and haughty duke in his splendid armor. All of them were grieved and ashamed that no one in that peaceful town could go out against him. All the lords and knights of King Ryence’s court came and stood in front of the King’s pavilion. They laughed and clapped their hands and cheered Duke Mordaunt as he rode up and down before them. The more they swelled with laughter, the more ashamed the people of Cameliard felt. “Ho! Ho!” cried the proud Duke. “What now! Will no one come out to meet me? How can you of Cameliard hope to face the King of North Wales and all his army of knights, when I am only one man among them?” And the people of Cameliard, gathered on the walls, listened to him with shame and sorrow.

All this time King Arthur had been digging in the garden. But he knew very well everything that was happening, and how the Duke of North Umber rode up and down so proudly before the castle walls. Suddenly he felt that he could not bear it any longer. So he put down his spade and slipped out by a small back gate, and went up into the town.

There was in Cameliard a very rich merchant named Ralph of Cardiff. The fame of his wealth and high standing had reached even King Arthur’s ears at Carleon. So King Arthur made his way to this man’s house.

In a narrow lane, not far from the merchant’s house, he took off his magic cap of disguise and took on something of his noble appearance again. He now wanted to show his knightliness to those who looked at him. So when he stood before the rich merchant in his private room, and the merchant looked up into his face, the merchant did not know what to think. Here was a lord of such noble bearing, dressed all in rough wool. King Arthur was a stranger to the good man, who did not know his face. Even so, the merchant knew that this was no ordinary knight. He must surely be a man of high rank and authority, even though he wore coarse cloth.

Then King Arthur opened the breast of his jerkin and showed the merchant the gold collar that hung around his neck. Under the rough woolen coat he also showed an undergarment of fine purple silk embroidered with gold. Then he showed the good man his own signet ring, and when the merchant saw it, he knew it was the ring of the King of Britain. Seeing these signs of high and lordly authority, the merchant rose, stood before the King, and took off his cap.

“Sir Merchant,” said the King, “know that I am a strange knight in disguise in this place. Even so, I can tell you that I am a very good friend to King Leodegrance and wish him well. Surely you know how the Duke of North Umber rides up and down before the King’s castle all the time, challenging anyone inside to come out and fight him for the Lady Guinevere. Now I mean to take up that fight myself, and I hope very much that I will uphold the honor of Cameliard and bring shame upon its enemies.

“Sir Merchant, I know very well that you have several suits of fine armor in your treasury. Their fame has reached my ears, though I live a good distance from here. So I ask you to outfit me in the best way you can, so that I may fight that Duke of North Umber right away. I give you my knightly word that you will be fully repaid for the best suit of armor you can lend me, and that it will be very soon.”

“My Lord,” said Master Ralph, “I can see that you are no ordinary wandering knight, but a man of very high rank. It is a great pleasure to carry out all your wishes. But even if you were someone other than you are, I would gladly give you armor, since you wish to ride out against that duke.”

With this he rang a little silver bell that stood near him, and several attendants came at once in answer to its sound. He placed the King in their hands and told them to show him the greatest honor. Some of the attendants prepared a bath of lukewarm water for the King, perfumed with ambergris, which felt very pleasant. After he had bathed and been dried with soft linen towels, other attendants led him to a hall hung all over with tapestries and embroideries. There a noble feast had been laid out for his refreshment. The lordly merchant himself looked after the King’s needs. He served him many kinds of fine, delicate meats, and also fine white bread. He poured him wines from various countries, some as red as rubies and others as yellow as gold. Indeed, the King had hardly ever enjoyed a better feast than the one Ralph of Cardiff spread for him.

When he had eaten and was fully refreshed, six pages came in, richly dressed in blue silk. They took the King to a grand room and dressed him in a suit of Spanish armor, very skillfully made and inlaid with gold. Its like could hardly be found anywhere in the land. The tunic worn over the armor and all the other trappings were of satin, as white as milk. The shield was white too, with no painted emblem or design of any kind. Then the attendants led the King into the courtyard, where a noble war-horse stood, as white as milk. All its trappings were of milk-white cloth, with no emblem or decoration of any kind. Its bridle and reins were studded all over with silver knobs.

The attendants helped King Arthur mount this horse. Then the lordly merchant came forward and gave him many words of encouragement. The King said farewell and rode away, shining in white and glittering in fine armor, so that he looked like the full moon in harvest season.
As he rode down the stony streets of the town, the people turned and gazed after him, for he made a very noble sight as he passed along the narrow way between the houses.

King Arthur rode to the back gate of the castle. There he got down from his horse and tied it. Then he went straight into the garden, and finding an attendant there, he asked to speak with the Lady Guinevere at once. The attendant, amazed at his lordly appearance, went and gave the message. Soon the Lady Guinevere came, full of wonder, and walked along a gallery with several of her damsels until she was above the place where King Arthur stood. When King Arthur looked up and saw her above him, he loved her very much. And he said to her, “Lady, I greatly wish to do you the honor I am able. I am going out now to fight that Duke of North Umber who rides up and down before this castle. I hope, and truly believe, that I will bring about his downfall. So I ask you for some token, such as a lady may give to a knight to wear when he rides out to do her honor.”

Then the Lady Guinevere said, “Truly, Sir Knight, I wish I knew who you are. Yet even though I do not know, I am quite willing to take you as my champion, as you offer. As for the token you speak of, if you tell me what you would like, I will gladly give it to you.”
“If that is so, Lady,” said King Arthur, “I would like the necklace you wear around your throat. It seems to me that if I had it tied around my arm, my courage would grow much greater.”

“By my faith, Sir Knight,” said the Lady, “you will surely have what you ask of me.” As she spoke, she took the necklace of pearls from her long, smooth neck and dropped it down to King Arthur where he stood.

King Arthur took the necklace and tied it around his arm, and he thanked her warmly. Then he bowed to the Lady Guinevere with true knightly grace, and she bowed to him. Then he went out from that place at once, his heart swelling with joy that the Lady Guinevere had shown him such favor.

By now the word had gone around Cameliard that a knight was going out to fight the Duke of North Umber. So great crowds gathered on the walls. King Leodegrance and the Lady Guinevere and the whole court came to the part of the castle walls that overlooked the meadow where the Duke of North Umber waited. Soon so great a crowd had gathered that any knight would be encouraged to do his very best before the many watchers looking down on the field.

Then suddenly the portcullis of the castle was raised and the drawbridge was let down, and the White Champion rode out to the fight he had taken on. As he rode across the narrow bridge, the hoofs of his war-horse struck the boards with a noise like thunder. When he came out into the sunlight, behold, his armor flashed like lightning, and when the people saw him, they shouted aloud.

When the Duke of North Umber saw a knight dressed all in white, he rode straight up to him and spoke words of knightly greeting. “Messire,” he said, “I see that you wear no crest on your helmet and no emblem on your shield, so I do not know who you are. Even so, I believe you are a knight of good quality and proven courage, or you would not have come to this place.”
“Truly, Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “I am of a rank equal to your own. And as for my courage, I believe it has been proven in as many fights as yours has.”

“Sir Knight,” said the Duke of Umber, “you speak with a very bold spirit. Even so, you may say whatever prayers you can, for I will soon knock you from your saddle so that you will never rise again. I have done the same to better men than you could ever hope to be.”
King Arthur answered this with great calm: “That will be as Heaven wills, Sir Knight, and not as you will.”

Then each knight saluted the other and rode to his place. There each one set his spear and shield and made himself ready for the fight. A silence fell over everyone, so deep that a man could hear his own heart beating. For a short while each knight sat like a statue made of iron. Then suddenly each one shouted to his war-horse, dug his spurs into its side, and shot forward from his place. They met in the middle of the course with a noise like a violent thunderclap. And behold, the spear of the Duke of North Umber burst into splinters, down to the very stump. But the spear of King Arthur did not break. It held firm, and the Duke was thrown out of his saddle like a windmill, whirling in the air. He struck the earth so hard that the ground shook beneath him. Indeed, he rolled over and over three full times before he stopped.
Then all the people on the wall shouted with all their might, so that the noise was astonishing. They had hardly hoped that their champion would prove so extraordinarily strong and skillful.

Meanwhile, the men of King Ryence’s court ran at once to the Duke of Umber where he lay on the ground, and they quickly unlaced his helmet to give him air. At first they thought he was dead, and then they thought he was about to die, for behold, he lay without any life or movement. He did not wake from that swoon for a full two hours and more.

While the attendants were busy with Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, King Arthur sat quietly on his horse and watched everything they did. Then he saw that his enemy was not dead. He turned his horse around and rode away from that place.

He did not go back to Cameliard at that time. He felt that he was not yet finished with these enemies of the peace of his realm. So he decided not to return the horse and armor to the merchant yet, but to keep them for a while in case he needed them again.

He remembered that on his way to Cameliard he had passed through a part of the forest where some woodcutters were chopping down trees. He thought he would go there and leave his horse and armor with those rough folk until he needed them again. So he rode off into the countryside. He left behind him the town, the castle, and all the noise of shouting and celebration. Not once did he turn his head to look back at the place where he had so mightily defeated his enemy.

Soon you will hear of some pleasant and happy adventures that happened to him before he had finished all he meant to do. A man who is a king among men, as King Arthur was, has such a calm and steady nature that neither victory nor defeat can change him. Victory does not make him too proud of himself, and defeat does not trouble his spirit so much that he falls into despair. So if you want to become like King Arthur, take all your triumphs the way he took this victory. You will not be turned away from your final purposes by the loud praise of many people. Instead, you will first finish the work you set yourself to do, and only then allow yourself to sit down and enjoy the rewards of your victory.
Yes, a true king of men does not say to himself, “Look! I deserve to be crowned with laurels.” Instead he says to himself, “What more can I do to make the world a better place through my efforts?”
